For phones with a picture bug, such as a black flash or black players. Change one at a time, restart the game, play a match, and capture it (CAPTURE) with what you saw. Put it back if it does not help. Takes effect at the next start.
Frame arena size in MB. Phones with a lot of memory use a large one by default; a smaller one is what the phones that look right use.
Draws with render passes and baked state, as older phones do, instead of dynamic rendering.
Shows the frame without the game\'s display colour table.
Lets the GPU decode BC textures itself instead of the CPU. Off by default on Qualcomm because of an old flicker.
Sets depth, stencil and culling per draw instead of baking them into pipelines (Qualcomm default is baked).

Shows the debug-only tools in a match: the CAPTURE button, the REC MACRO button beside Menu, macro play in the pause menu, the HUD\u2019s detail card and console, and the test options below. Leave off to play.

The readout in the top-left corner of a match. Minimal: frames per second. Normal: adds frame time and temperature. Complete: adds CPU, memory and textures on a second line. Also in a match: pause and choose \u201cPerformance HUD\u201d.

Drag a control to move it, pinch it or use the size slider to resize it, and hide the ones you do not use. A control dropped on another steps aside. Also in a match: pause and choose \u201cEdit controls\u201d.
Touch a control to pick it up
For tinkering and troubleshooting. The defaults suit most phones; the Graphics and Performance tabs cover the usual changes.
Every change is kept the moment it is made, and takes effect when the next match starts. Press Back to return to the menu.

This phone looks like %1$s (%2$s; %3$s, %4$d fast cores at %5$d MHz, %6$.1f GB). A preset sets render quality, the heat and GPU-load rules, multisampling, FSR, the frame-rate limit and low-memory mode; change any of them afterwards and the preset reads Custom.
How many pixels are drawn on the screen, as a share of it. The display scales the result up. PES draws at a fixed 1280\u00d7720, so this mostly trades sharpness for battery.
Draws the match at 2x or 3x the console\u2019s 1280\u00d7720 (PES17_SCALE). Needs a lot of GPU; leave at 1x unless the phone has room to spare.
Keeps thin pitch lines from breaking into dashes. Cheap on most phones; turn it off if the match stutters.
The console\u2019s frame is a 60 Hz frame. Locking avoids uneven pacing and saves battery on 90/120 Hz screens.
Draws the match ball this much larger so it is easier to follow on a small screen (PES17_BALL_SCALE). 100% is the original size.

How large the 3D scene is drawn before it is stretched to the frame (PES17_SCENE_SCALE). 75% is the default: about 44% fewer pixels for a picture most players cannot tell apart. Go to 100% on a strong phone.

Match render quality above becomes the most the picture is drawn at. As Android reports the phone heating up (moderate, severe, critical) the picture is lowered, down to 50%, before the GPU is throttled, and raised again as it cools (PES17_HEAT_SCALE). Steps are held a few seconds; one shows as the scene being redrawn for a moment.
Lower quality when the GPU falls behind

Steps the picture down when the render passes take too long for the frame and back up when there is room (PES17_LOAD_SCALE). It only sees GPU pass time, which on the Snapdragon 865 was not what made a slow match slow, so it rarely acts there. Experimental.

Tells Android how long each frame took so it can raise or lower the CPU and GPU clock (PES17_HINT). Does nothing on a phone that refuses it, such as the Snapdragon 865 on Android 13; turn it off if a phone runs hotter with it.

Off leaves the stands empty and spares the renderer and the GPU the crowd\u2019s drawing, which keeps the phone a little cooler in a match. The game still animates it. Takes effect the next time the game starts.

For phones where the picture flashes black on every third frame: a lone black frame is replaced by the frame before it. Reads every frame back, so it costs speed. Takes effect at the next start of the game.
Uses an AMD FSR upscale and sharpen pass instead of a plain stretch. Costs a few frames on a hot phone.

The game draws 30 frames a second and a frame made between each two fills the gaps, so the 60 Hz screen stays smooth for about half the work and heat. Fast movement can look soft. Sets the 30 fps limit while on.

Widens the game\'s camera to the phone\'s shape and fills the whole screen instead of showing black bars at the sides (PES17_ASPECT). Menus and the score bar are stretched sideways. Takes effect on the next start.
Match the screen to the frame limit

Asks the display for the rate the match is paced at: a 30 fps limit on a 30 Hz mode is one screen tick per frame, so the phone stops showing every frame twice and the picture arrives a little sooner. Phones with no such mode keep the one they are on. Ignored while frame generation is on, which needs 60 Hz.

Auto picks the best this phone supports. At a 30 FPS limit, Smooth schedules every frame on an even display refresh: display timing (VK_GOOGLE_display_timing) where the driver offers it, otherwise a pacer locked to the display phase measured from presented frames. Compatibility restores the original presentation. Applies when the next match starts; a frame-pacing change never alters the quality preset or its settings.

Only affects a 30 FPS match. System default keeps the choices above: match the screen to the frame limit, or the 60 Hz lock. Prefer 60 Hz keeps 30 FPS on every second refresh of a 60 Hz screen, which is what display-timing pacing schedules on. Disabled while frame generation is on, which needs 60 Hz.

How much filtering the game\u2019s textures may use at a glancing angle, where the pitch runs to the horizon (PES17_MAX_ANISO). Android already caps it at 4x; 2x or 1x is cheaper on a phone losing frames in wide camera shots, 8x or 16x sharper on one with room to spare.

Takes the match off the 60 Hz pacing and limits it to this many frames a second (PES17_FPS_LIMIT). Lower is cooler and longer-lasting. On a 60 Hz screen 30 gives the most even motion; 35 to 55 can judder.
Skips the large vertex shadow buffer (PES17_NO_SHADOW). Use it on 6 GB phones or less, or if the match is killed in the background.
Texture memory: chosen for this phone
How much the texture cache may hold before it lets go of what has not been drawn lately. Left alone, the runtime picks a figure from this phone\u2019s memory.
Compiles every recorded pipeline before the title screen instead of during play. Boot takes minutes on a cold cache, but kick-off is free of shader stutter afterwards.
Touch controls stay player 1; the first physical controller drives player 2. Takes effect when a match is started.
Turn off to ignore controllers entirely. Some phones report an accessory as a gamepad with a stick that is not centred, which makes a player run on his own.

During a match the d-pad fades out after four seconds without a touch, and comes back the moment you tap where it sits. In the title\'s menus it always stays visible. Turn this off to keep it on screen permanently.
Soft glow and a short press animation on the pad. Turn off if the pad feels heavy or the phone runs warm.

Read feints from the flick of your thumb instead of its position on the stick. Eight directions, with a moment of nothing between them, so \"left, then right\" is two moves rather than one circle. Turn off for the older stick that follows the thumb exactly.
Move puts the stick wherever your thumb lands on the left of the screen and follows it, as eFootball does; Fixed keeps it where the layout put it. Either way the knob you see is the throw.
Bring out the controls arranged for defending instead of the attacking ones. The title does not report who has the ball, so this is your own switch.
The on-screen pad is edited in the match: pause and choose \u201cEdit controls\u201d.
The files stay on the phone; the app simply stops using them, and a new folder can be chosen. If the files are still in a place the app searches, it will find them again on its own.

Everything the pad can do, read from the controls you are using now.

Left thumb: move. The stick floats to where you land on the left half, or stays in its socket if you prefer it fixed. Push it to the rim to sprint: that works on the normal stick and only while a match is on screen, and the run holds until you pull back inside the release point. The two-stage stick gives the throw a longer reach and no sprint, so it can be used at the title\'s own menus. Right thumb: the action diamond. The d-pad above the stick is for tactics; it fades after three quiet seconds and comes back when you tap, or slide a thumb, where it sits.
Roll a thumb between pass, cross, shoot and through ball without lifting: the direction you leave in is read as a swipe. Hold RB and centre the stick to dummy. Tap RB twice for the burst.
Hold SKILL for a moment and a ring of eight moves opens under your thumb. Slide into a sector and lift. A quick tap does nothing, so a resting thumb cannot set off a feint.

Choose the defending pad in Settings, Controls. The action buttons keep their positions and gain a second label: press, team, slide and goalkeeper. The near-thumb LB switches player; the far LB is the attacking copy.

Each action button, spare and tactical button sends a different command in each of its four directions. Select one and tap Swipe directions: each direction opens a group first — nothing, the pad\'s buttons, double taps, a held modifier with a face button (L1 + pass, R2 + shoot), a full flick of the left or right stick, or a modifier with a stick flick — then the entries in that group. A bound direction is sent when the thumb lifts: a plain button as a single press, a combination or a stick flick as a short held sequence, a double tap as two presses. The arrows on the rim show what is bound, and the editor warns when a track is blocked. L1 and R1 are modifiers, so they carry no swipes of their own.

Ten spare buttons ship hidden: faded circles along the top of the editor, off the pad until you give one a job. Select one and bind its centre tap and its four swipes, and it joins the pad. The tactical pair is SW1 and ADV (advanced instructions: hold LT and use the d-pad arms). L1 and R1 stay modifiers — L1 + pass, R1 + shoot — rather than swipe targets, and double-tapping pass plays the one-two.

Pause and choose Edit controls, or open Settings, Controls, Arrange controls. Drag the selected control, and use the strip at the bottom: the sliders resize and fade it, the switch hides it, Save Layout and Layouts save, load or share the pad, and Swipe directions and Skill wheel bind what it sends. With a control selected, More offers Bind, Rename, Remove, Undo and Redo; with nothing selected it offers Add a control, Profiles, Export, Import, Undo and Redo. Reset one and Reset all sit beside Done, and Restore default controls is always one tap away.

In a match, Menu pauses the game and opens Carry on, Edit controls, Controls guide, the touch-pad and gamepad switches, Quick graphics, the HUD level and Quit; the match stays paused until you leave the menu or the editor. Before a match, the launcher offers Play, Install game, Graphics driver, Settings, View log and Check for updates. Settings holds Controls, Graphics & performance and Advanced; Bring out the defending pad, Arrange controls and the default-controls restore live under Controls.
A touch belongs to the control it lands on until that finger lifts. Movement never becomes a shot, a swipe belongs to the button it started on, and no control holds a bit it does not show.

A PES 2017 data pack is either the .cpk archives plus DpFileList.bin, or the Xbox 360 content packages (CON / LIVE / PIRS) the community ships, for title 0x4A3007D1. Its CPKs, DpFileList and edit save are read from inside the packages. The pack is written to dlc/SYSTEM00000000 beside the game, which the runtime mounts at launch; the game folder itself is never changed. A locked archive asks for its password, and the password is not kept.
